title: Laverbread
subtitle: traditional Welsh cooked seaweed
excerpt: Laverbread is cooked and pureed laver seaweed, a traditional Welsh food eaten as a side dish, particularly with bacon and cockles as part of a Welsh breakfast. The flavour is intensely savoury, like a mineral-rich spinach. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Laverbread (bara lawr in Welsh) has been eaten in Wales for centuries, gathered from the rocky shores of the Gower Peninsula, Carmarthen Bay, and around Pembrokeshire. It is mentioned in travellers' accounts of Wales from the 17th century onwards. Lady Llanover (Augusta Hall), The First Principles of Good Cookery (1867, National Library of Wales), describes laverbread as a staple of the Welsh diet eaten with oatcakes or served alongside bacon. S. Minwel Tibbott, Welsh Fare (1976, National Museum of Wales), gives detailed instructions for both home preparation from raw laver and the use of tinned laverbread, which has been sold commercially since the early 20th century and is the form most commonly available today.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Laverbread can be bought ready-prepared in cans or as fresh packs from Welsh fishmongers and delis. Starting from raw laver requires 4 to 6 hours of initial simmering.

glossaryTerms.definition: Porphyra umbilicalis, a purple-black seaweed harvested from Atlantic and Irish Sea coasts. Once boiled for several hours it reduces to a smooth, dark green-black paste with an intense umami flavour. Available commercially in Wales as tinned or fresh-pack laverbread.

content.text: Laverbread, despite its name, is not a bread. It is cooked and pureed

, dark green-black and intensely savoury. The simplest way to serve it is heated through in a pan with a little butter and a squeeze of lemon, alongside bacon, cockles, and toast as part of a traditional Welsh breakfast. On its own it looks alarming but tastes good: mineral, umami-rich, somewhere between spinach and oysters.

Most people start with commercially prepared laverbread, sold in cans or fresh packs at Welsh fishmongers, delis, and online. The recipe below uses prepared laverbread. If starting from raw fresh laver seaweed, it must be simmered for 4 to 6 hours first until it collapses to a paste.

items.prepNote: prepared, from a tin or fresh pack

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small frying pan over a medium heat. Add {{laverbread}} of prepared laverbread and stir to combine with the butter.
Cook for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring frequently, until the laverbread is heated through and slightly concentrated. It should hold its shape in the pan but remain spreadable.

Season with {{lemon-juice}} of lemon juice, {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt, and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper. Taste: laverbread varies in saltiness by brand. Serve alongside grilled or fried bacon rashers and warm cockles, with toast.

items.cause: Tinned laverbread can be high in natural sea salt from the seaweed
items.fix: Taste before seasoning. Reduce or omit added salt. A squeeze of lemon helps balance an over-salty batch.

items.symptom: Laverbread dries out and sticks to the pan
items.cause: Heat too high or cooked for too long
items.fix: Use a medium heat and stir frequently. Add a splash of water if it starts to stick.

content.text: Laverbread is the most distinctively Welsh food there is. It appears on every traditional Welsh breakfast plate, alongside bacon, cockles, and soda bread. In the mining communities of south Wales it was gathered by hand from the shoreline and eaten for its mineral content as much as its flavour. Today it is sold in Welsh delis and fishmongers, and Richard Burton reportedly declared it the food he missed most when abroad. The flavour takes some getting used to; once acquired, it is like nothing else.
